1% rule: Quick screen: monthly rent should be at least 1% of the price. A filter, not a buy signal — it ignores taxes, insurance, and vacancy.
100 hours and more than anyone else: A material-participation test met by working over 100 hours and more than any other person on the property.
100% bonus depreciation: Writing off the entire cost of qualifying property in the year you put it to use.
1014: The tax code section providing the step-up in basis to fair market value at death.
1031: A like-kind exchange that defers capital-gains tax when proceeds are reinvested into another investment property.
1031 exchange: A like-kind exchange that defers capital-gains tax when you roll proceeds into another investment property.
1031 exchanges: Swaps of one investment property for another that postpone capital-gains tax.
1031 like-kind exchange: Swapping one investment property for another similar one so you do not pay capital gains tax right away.
1040-ES: The IRS form for paying estimated quarterly taxes once income is no longer withheld from a paycheck.
1099 obligations: The duty to report certain payments you make to vendors using IRS 1099 forms.
1099-NEC: The form you must issue to unincorporated contractors paid over the threshold ($2,000 for 2026).
199A: The tax-code section for the 20% qualified-business-income deduction, made permanent by OBBBA.
2% rule: Aggressive screen: rent at least 2% of price. Rare today and usually only in higher-risk areas.
27.5-year: The number of years over which residential rental buildings are depreciated for taxes.
39-year: The number of years over which commercial buildings are depreciated for taxes.
401(k): An employer retirement plan; capture the match before stretching into real estate.
50% rule: Rule of thumb that operating expenses run about 50% of gross rent (excluding the mortgage).
500 hours: One material-participation test, met by working at least 500 hours in the activity during the year.
7-day average: The rule that if guests stay an average of seven days or less, the property is treated as a business not a rental.
70% rule: BRRRR guardrail — keep your all-in cost (purchase + rehab) near 70% of the after-repair value.
721 exchange: Contributing property into a REIT operating partnership for OP units, tax-deferred (an UPREIT).
75% rule (rental income): Lenders count only 75 percent of a property's gross rent as income when qualifying you, to allow for vacancy and expenses.
absentee owner: A property owner who does not live in or near the property, often a target for off-market offers.
absentee owners: Property owners who do not live in or near the property they own.
ACA: Affordable Care Act — marketplace health insurance to budget for if you leave a W-2 job.
ACA marketplace: The government health-insurance exchange where you buy your own coverage if you lack an employer plan.
accredited investor: A person who meets income or wealth rules letting them invest in certain private deals.
acquisition: The act of buying a property.
acquisition debt: The loan you took out to buy, build, or improve a home, which limits how much mortgage interest you can deduct.
active participation: A lower bar than material participation that can unlock up to $25k of rental losses against ordinary income.
actual cash value: Insurance that pays the depreciated value of damaged property, subtracting for age and wear, so an old roof is reimbursed as old.
additional insured: A party added to someone else's insurance policy so they are also protected by it, such as you on a contractor's policy.
adequate capitalization: Keeping enough money in an LLC to cover its obligations, since an empty shell entity is easy for a court to disregard.
advance rate: The share of your portfolio a lender will lend against — often 50–70% for diversified stocks.
adverse-action notice: A required notice telling an applicant you denied or charged them more partly because of a report.
AFR: Applicable federal rate — the minimum interest the IRS requires on a seller-financed (installment) note.
after-repair value: What a property will be worth after renovation — the number a BRRRR refinance is based on.
AGI: Adjusted gross income — income after certain deductions; drives many tax thresholds.
AirDNA: A tool that estimates short-term rental (Airbnb) income for an area.
allocate basis: To divide a property purchase price between the land portion and the building portion.
allowed or allowable: Rule that recapture applies to the depreciation you should have taken, even if you forgot to claim it.
amended returns: Revised past tax returns; Form 3115 lets you fix depreciation without filing these.
amortization: The gradual paydown of loan principal through your payments; tenants effectively build your equity over time.
AMT: Alternative minimum tax — a parallel tax a huge bonus-depreciation year or large ISO exercise can still trigger.
ancillary income: Extra income beyond base rent, such as fees for pets, parking, laundry, or storage.
annual debt service: A full year of mortgage principal and interest payments.
annual gift exclusion: The amount you can give each person each year without using up your lifetime exemption or owing gift tax.
anonymity: Keeping your ownership of property private, achievable in certain states or through structures like land trusts.
anti-deficiency laws: State laws that limit or block a lender from pursuing you for the shortfall after a foreclosure.
applicable federal rate: The minimum IRS-set interest rate a private loan must charge to avoid tax problems.
appraisal: A professional estimate of a property value, sometimes used to allocate basis.
appraisal gap: The shortfall when a property appraises for less than expected, which directly shrinks how much cash you can pull out.
appraised value: The value a professional appraiser assigns to a property, which the refinance lender relies on.
appreciating real estate: Property expected to grow in value, which should not be held in an S-corp or C-corp.
appreciation: The increase in a property value over time.
appreciation plays: Properties bought mainly hoping their value rises, rather than for monthly income.
appreciation-only: An investment whose only return comes from rising value, with no income along the way.
APR: Annual percentage rate — a loan's yearly cost including certain fees, usually a bit above the note rate.
ARV: After-repair value — what the property is worth once renovated. The basis the BRRRR refinance lends against.
asbestos: A hazardous old building material that is costly and risky to remove.
assessor ratio: The land-to-building value split from the local tax assessor, used to allocate basis.
asset: Something you own that has value, like cash, stocks, or real estate.
asset allocation: How you divide your money among different types of investments.
asset class: A category of investment, such as real estate, stocks, or bonds, that tends to behave similarly.
asset location: Deciding which accounts (taxable vs. tax-advantaged) to hold each investment in for tax efficiency.
asset-based: A loan decision driven mainly by the value of the property being financed rather than the borrower's income.
asset-holding LLC: A company whose only job is to own a property, kept separate from the management entity.
assistance/service animals: Animals a disabled tenant needs, which are not pets and cannot be banned or charged pet fees.
auctions: Public sales where properties go to the highest bidder, often with limited inspection.
audit target: A tax position the IRS is especially likely to examine closely.
audit triggers: Tax return features that make the IRS more likely to examine you.
audited financial statement: A formal financial report reviewed by an accountant; not needed for the smaller de minimis deduction limit.
Augusta rule: §280A(g): rent your personal home to your business up to 14 days a year and the income is tax-free.
automated underwriting: A lender's computer system that evaluates and approves a loan application against set rules.
bad-boy carve-outs: Clauses that flip a non-recourse loan to full recourse if you commit fraud, transfer the property, etc.
balance sheet: A snapshot of what you own and what you owe, used to gauge financial health.
ballast: A steadying element in a portfolio that keeps it stable when conditions get rough.
balloon: A loan that requires a large lump-sum payoff of the remaining balance on a set date, usually by refinancing or selling.
balloon-maturity risk: The danger that a balloon loan comes due when no lender will refinance it, forcing a sale or default.
basis: The amount the tax system says you have invested in a property, used to figure your taxable gain.
basis schedule: A running record of a property cost and adjustments used to calculate gain and depreciation.
basis step-up: An increase in your investment basis that reduces the taxable gain.
beneficial interest: The ownership benefit of a property held in a trust, which can be assigned to an LLC while the trust holds legal title.
beneficial ownership: The identity of the actual individuals who own or control a company, which some reporting rules require disclosing.
beneficiary: The person who receives the benefit of property held in a trust.
BiggerPockets: A popular online community and resource hub for real estate investors.
blanket loan: One loan covering several properties via cross-collateralization.
blow-up: A financial collapse where an investor loses much or all of what they built.
BOI: Beneficial ownership information — the FinCEN report on who owns an entity (domestic LLCs currently exempt).
bonded: A contractor backed by a surety bond, a financial guarantee that pays out if they fail to complete or properly do the work.
bonus depreciation: Deducting a large share of qualifying assets in year one; restored to 100% by OBBBA for property placed in service after Jan 19, 2025.
bookkeeping: The ongoing recording of your income, expenses, and financial transactions.
boot: Cash or debt relief received in a 1031 exchange — it is taxable up to the amount of your gain.
brackets: The income ranges that determine your tax rate; spreading income can keep you in lower ones.
break-even: The point where income exactly equals expenses, with no profit or loss.
bridge financing: Short-term borrowing meant to be repaid quickly, used to cover a gap until permanent financing or cash arrives.
brokerage: An account or firm through which you buy and sell investments like stocks and funds.
brokerage account: An account you use to buy and sell investments like stocks and funds.
BRRRR: Buy, Rehab, Rent, Refinance, Repeat — force value through renovation, then cash-out refinance to recycle your capital into the next deal.
build-to-suit exchange: A 1031 variation where exchange money funds construction on the replacement property.
builder's risk: Insurance for a vacant or under-renovation property, when a standard landlord policy often voids coverage.
builder's-risk coverage: Insurance covering a property while it is being renovated or built.
builders-risk: Insurance covering a property during renovation, when a standard landlord policy may not apply.
business expense: A cost of running a business that you can deduct from income, lowering your tax.
buy borrow die: A strategy of buying assets, borrowing against them tax-free for cash, then dying so heirs get a step-up that erases the gain.
C-corp: A C corporation — double-taxed and a trap for real estate (no step-up, trapped gains). Do not hold property in one.
CA-source gain: Profit tied to a California property that California can still tax later.
California clawback: A rule where California taxes a deferred gain from a CA property even after you exchange into another state and move away.
cancellation-of-debt: Forgiven debt that the IRS can treat as taxable income (e.g., after a short sale or foreclosure).
cancellation-of-debt income: Taxable income that can arise when debt is wiped out for less than its balance, such as after a foreclosure or short sale.
cap rate: Capitalization rate = NOI ÷ price. The unlevered yield; use it to compare properties regardless of financing. A higher cap usually means higher risk, not a better deal.
CapEx: Capital expenditures — big, infrequent replacements like roof, HVAC, and water heater that you reserve for.
CapEx reserve: Money saved for big, infrequent replacements like a roof or HVAC system.
capital: The money you have available to invest or put into a deal.
capital expenditures: Large, infrequent replacements (roof, HVAC, etc.) — budget a monthly reserve for them.
capital gains: The taxable profit you make when you sell an asset for more than you paid.
capital gains tax: The tax you owe on the profit from selling an investment like property or stock.
capital improvement: A major upgrade that adds lasting value to a property and increases its basis.
capitalization rate: NOI ÷ price — the unlevered yield used to compare properties regardless of how they are financed.
capitalize: To add a cost to a property basis and deduct it slowly over years, rather than all at once.
carrier: The insurance company that issues your policy and pays claims.
carry forward: To move an unused loss or deduction into future tax years.
carrying costs: The ongoing expenses of owning a property, such as mortgage, taxes, and insurance, owed whether or not it earns income.
carryover basis: When an assets original cost basis transfers to the new owner unchanged, instead of resetting to current value.
cash flow: The money left over each month after operating expenses and the mortgage are paid.
cash flow out of the gate: Earning a monthly profit right from the start of ownership.
cash reserves: Money kept readily available to cover living costs and property surprises.
cash-equivalents: Very safe holdings that act almost like cash, such as money-market funds.
cash-flowing property: A property whose rent more than covers all its costs, leaving you a monthly profit.
cash-on-cash: Annual pre-tax cash flow ÷ the actual cash you put in — your levered return. Roughly 8–12% is considered solid.
cash-out refi: Refinancing into a larger loan to take cash out — best when your current rate is not far below market.
cash-out refinance: Replacing your mortgage with a larger one and pocketing the difference in cash; it resets your whole loan.
cash-out refinancing: Refinancing for a larger loan than you owe and pocketing the difference in cash.
cast-iron drains: Old metal drain pipes that rust and crack with age.
certificate of insurance: A document from an insurer confirming a contractor's coverage, ideally sent directly by the carrier and naming you as protected.
CFPB: Consumer Financial Protection Bureau — regulator behind FCRA tenant-screening and adverse-action rules.
change order: A documented, priced change to the original renovation plan, agreed in writing before the extra work proceeds.
change-of-control notification: A loan requirement that you tell the lender if ownership or control of the borrowing entity changes.
change-order discipline: The practice of pricing and signing off on every deviation from the plan before the work is done, to control costs.
charging order: The core LLC asset-protection rule: a member creditor can only reach distributions, not the LLC assets.
charging-order protection: The legal shield that limits a member's creditor to a charging order, keeping them from taking control of the LLC's assets.
charitable deduction: A tax write-off you get for donating money or property to charity.
Charitable Remainder Trust: A trust you donate appreciated property to; it sells tax-free, pays you income, and leaves the rest to charity.
child LLC: A subsidiary LLC, typically owning one property, used to wall off that property's risk from the rest of the portfolio.
Class A: The highest-quality neighborhoods and properties, with the best tenants and lowest returns.
Class B: Solid middle-class properties seen as a sweet spot balancing income and hassle.
Class C: Older working-class properties with more upkeep, turnover, and fragile cash flow.
Class D: The roughest areas, with high vacancy and problems, that rarely deliver promised income.
class life: The number of years the IRS assigns to a type of property for depreciation purposes.
cliff: A tax rule where crossing a limit suddenly removes a benefit entirely, with no gradual phase-out.
closing costs: The various fees paid to finalize a property purchase, on top of the down payment.
co-host: A helper who manages a short-term rental with you; their hours count against your participation test.
COD income: Cancellation-of-debt income — forgiven debt that can be taxed, often right when you are already underwater.
collateral: An asset you pledge to back a loan, which the lender can take if you do not repay.
combined LTV: The total of all loans against a property divided by its value, counting both the first mortgage and any second loan like a HELOC.
combined scenario: A stress test that hits every property with multiple shocks at once, instead of testing one variable in isolation.
commingle: To improperly mix tenant deposit money or business funds with your personal money.
commingled: Mixing business and personal money in one account, which is risky for taxes and legal protection.
commingling: Mixing personal and business money — the most common reason an LLC shield gets pierced.
community property: In certain states, assets acquired during a marriage are owned jointly by both spouses regardless of whose name is on title.
community property states: States like California, Texas, and Washington where marital assets are treated as jointly owned and get special tax treatment.
community-property states: States where assets acquired during a marriage are generally owned jointly regardless of whose name is on title.
compounded daily: Interest that is added every day, so the amount owed grows a little each day.
compounding: When your earnings themselves generate earnings over time, accelerating growth.
comps: Comparable properties used to estimate a property's value or rent.
concentration: Having too much of your money tied up in one type of asset or area, which raises risk.
concentration ceiling: Your self-imposed cap on real estate plus leverage as a share of total net worth (counting home equity).
constructive receipt: Touching or controlling the sale proceeds yourself — it disqualifies a 1031 exchange.
consumer reports: Credit or background reports on a person, governed by federal law when used to screen tenants.
contemporaneous records: Records created at the time events happen, which hold up far better in an audit than ones made later.
contemporaneous time logs: Records of your hours kept as you go, used to prove how much you worked on real estate.
contested eviction: An eviction the tenant fights in court, which can drag on and cost a lot.
contingency: Extra money (often 10 to 15 percent) set aside in a rehab budget to cover surprises and overruns.
conventional financing: Standard mortgage loans that follow common guidelines and usually require proof of personal income.
conventional investment-property mortgag: A standard bank loan to buy a rental property, with stricter terms than a loan on a home you live in.
conventional loan: A standard mortgage not backed by a government agency, following Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac guidelines.
conventional program: A standard mortgage following Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac rules, as opposed to a government-insured FHA loan.
correlated assets: Investments that tend to rise and fall together, so they fail to cushion each other in a downturn.
correlated shock: When several troubles strike at once because they share a common cause, rather than arriving one at a time.
correlation: The tendency of different risks or assets to move together, so problems pile up simultaneously in a downturn.
cost basis: What you originally paid for an asset plus improvements, used to figure taxable gain when you sell.
cost seg: A study that breaks a building into shorter-life parts so you can accelerate depreciation.
cost segregation: An engineering study that reclassifies building parts into shorter lives to front-load depreciation.
cost-seg study: An engineering report that reclassifies building components to speed up depreciation deductions.
county assessor: The local government office that values properties and holds ownership records.
CPA: Certified Public Accountant — the tax pro you want to be a real-estate specialist.
credit and background check: A review of an applicant's borrowing history and any criminal or court records.
cross-collateralization: Using multiple properties to secure one loan — a single default can put all of them at risk.
CRT: Charitable remainder trust — donate appreciated property; it sells tax-free, pays you income, remainder to charity.
cushion: Extra money or margin kept on hand to absorb an unexpected problem.
daily liquidity: The ability to buy or sell an investment any business day.
de minimis safe harbor: A rule letting you immediately deduct low-cost items up to a set dollar amount per item or invoice.
de-risking: Deliberately lowering your risk, such as by paying down debt or building cash.
deal sourcing: The work of finding properties worth buying.
debt paydown: Steadily reducing what you owe on a loan.
debt relief: When a sale leaves you owing less debt than before; in a 1031 this counts as taxable boot.
debt service: The principal-and-interest payments owed on the loan.
debt service coverage ratio: NOI ÷ annual loan payments. Above 1.0 means the property more than covers its mortgage.
debt-free sleeve: A portion of your portfolio kept entirely free of loans as a safety anchor.
debt-to-income: Monthly debt ÷ gross monthly income; lenders use it to size how much you can borrow.
decreasing-term: A life insurance policy whose payout shrinks over time, often sized to track a declining loan balance.
deed: The legal document that transfers ownership of real estate from one party to another.
deed-in-lieu: Handing a property's deed back to the lender to avoid foreclosure.
default: Failing to make required loan payments, which can lead the lender to foreclose.
defer: To legally delay paying a tax until a later date instead of paying it now.
defer capital gains: To legally postpone paying tax on your investment profit until a future date.
deferred maintenance: Repairs that were put off and now pile up as future costs.
deficiency judgment: A personal judgment for the gap between the foreclosure sale price and what you owed.
Delaware Statutory Trust: A passive, fractional interest in institutional property used to keep deferring via 1031 without active management.
delinquency: Tenants falling behind on rent payments.
deposit held: The security deposit money currently being kept on a tenant's behalf.
depreciation: A yearly non-cash deduction for wear on the building (27.5 yrs residential) that shelters rental income.
depreciation recapture: Tax (up to 25%) on the depreciation you took — or could have taken — owed when you sell.
depreciation schedule: A record tracking how much depreciation you have claimed on a property each year.
direct mail: Sending letters or postcards to property owners to find sellers.
disability insurance: Coverage that replaces your income if illness or injury prevents you from working and managing the portfolio.
discrimination claims: Legal complaints that a landlord treated an applicant unfairly based on a protected trait.
disparate-impact: When a neutral policy ends up unfairly affecting a protected group, a basis for discrimination claims.
distressed properties: Properties in poor condition or owned by sellers under financial pressure.
distributions: Money paid out to business owners that, in an S-corp, avoids the 15.3 percent payroll tax.
diversification: Spreading money across different investments so one loss does not sink the whole portfolio.
diversify: To spread your money across different investments so one loss cannot sink you.
doors: Individual rental units; investors often count portfolio size in doors.
double leverage: Borrowing against one borrowed-against asset, such as using a loan on your stocks to fund a leveraged property purchase.
double step-up: In community property states, the full basis reset both spouses shares get when the first spouse dies.
double-entry: A bookkeeping method that records every transaction in two places to keep the books balanced.
down payment: The upfront cash you pay toward a purchase, with the rest covered by a loan.
DP-1: A basic landlord policy paying actual cash value (depreciated) on named perils only.
DP-3: A landlord dwelling policy paying replacement cost on an open-perils basis — get this over DP-1.
drag: Anything, like taxes or fees, that quietly reduces your investment returns over time.
draw period: The early years of a HELOC when you can borrow and repay freely, often paying interest only.
draw schedule: Paying a contractor in stages tied to completed, inspected work — so you never pay too much up front.
drawdown: A decline in the value of your assets from their peak, the loss you must be able to absorb in a downturn.
driving for dollars: Physically driving neighborhoods to spot neglected properties whose owners might sell.
dry powder: Available cash and liquid reserves you can deploy when needed, especially during a crisis.
DSCR: Debt service coverage ratio = NOI ÷ annual debt service. 1.0 is break-even; lenders usually want 1.20 or more.
DSCR loan: An investor loan that qualifies on the property cash flow (DSCR) instead of your personal income or DTI.
DSCR loans: Loans approved based on a property's rental income rather than your personal income.
DST: Delaware Statutory Trust — a passive, fractional interest in institutional real estate that qualifies for a 1031 exchange.
DSUE: Deceased spousal unused exclusion — unused estate-tax exemption a surviving spouse can inherit (file Form 706 to claim it).
DTI: Debt-to-income = your monthly debt ÷ gross monthly income. Conventional loans cap it around 43–50%.
DTI exhaustion: When your debt payments grow so large relative to income that lenders will not approve any more conventional loans.
dual vs. single earner: Whether a household has two incomes or relies on just one.
due diligence: The investigation you do before buying to confirm a property is really as good as it looks.
due-on-sale: A loan clause letting the lender demand full repayment if you transfer the property (e.g., into an LLC).
due-on-sale clause: A loan provision allowing the lender to call the full balance due if ownership of the property is transferred.
duplex: A building with two separate living units.
durable holdings: Investments built to survive bad times, typically with less debt against them.
durable power of attorney: A legal document letting a trusted person act on your behalf, including running your entities, if you become incapacitated.
dwelling policy: An insurance policy built for a rental or non-owner-occupied home, in forms labeled DP-1 or DP-3.
earnest money: A deposit you put down to show you are serious about buying a property.
earnest money goes hard: The point at which your deposit becomes non-refundable if you back out.
earthquake coverage: Separate insurance for earthquake damage, which standard property policies exclude even outside California.
easements: Legal rights allowing someone else to use part of your property, like a shared driveway.
EAT: Exchange Accommodation Titleholder — the party that 'parks' title in a reverse 1031 exchange.
EIN: Employer identification number — a federal tax ID; each LLC should have its own for clean separation.
emergency cushion: Savings kept aside specifically to handle unexpected financial shocks.
employer 401(k) match: Free money your employer adds to your retirement account when you contribute, up to a limit.
entitled: Land that has received the government approvals and permits needed to develop it for a specific use.
entitled land: Land already approved by the government for development, which can command higher value for patient investors.
entity: A legal business structure like an LLC that holds property and keeps its own books.
entity structuring: Setting up legal business entities, like LLCs, to hold and protect your properties.
EPA: Environmental Protection Agency — requires lead-based-paint disclosure on pre-1978 housing.
equity: The part of the property you actually own — its value minus what you still owe.
equity cushion: The buffer of ownership value you hold above what you owe, protecting you if prices fall.
equity cushion early: The thin slice of ownership you have soon after buying with a small down payment.
escrow: A neutral third party or account that holds money or documents until a deal or obligation is completed.
estate management LLC: The idea of separating property operations into their own company so operational lawsuits hit an entity holding little value.
estate tax: A federal tax on the value of assets you pass at death above the lifetime exemption, topping out at 40 percent.
estimated quarterly taxes: Tax payments you send the IRS four times a year when income is not withheld from a paycheck.
estoppel: A signed tenant statement confirming the real rent, deposit, and lease terms on an occupied building.
estoppel certificate: A tenant-signed confirmation of actual rent, deposit, and lease terms — verify it before buying occupied property.
ETF: An exchange-traded fund, a basket of investments that trades on a stock exchange like a single stock.
eviction: The legal process of removing a tenant who breaks the lease, such as by not paying rent.
eviction-history search: Checking whether an applicant has been evicted before.
Exchange Accommodation Titleholder: An entity that temporarily holds title to a property in a reverse exchange while you sell the old one.
executor: The person responsible for settling a deceased persons estate, including filing required tax forms.
fair housing: Laws barring discrimination against protected classes when renting; uniform, documented screening is the protection.
fair market value: The price a property would sell for between a willing buyer and seller, neither under pressure.
fair-market rate: The normal price something would rent or sell for in the open market.
fair-rental-value: Insurance that pays the rent you would have collected while a property is being repaired after a covered loss.
familial status: A protected class covering households with children, that you cannot discriminate against.
Fannie Mae: A government-sponsored company that buys mortgages from lenders and sets the rules most standard loans must follow.
Fannie/Freddie: Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, government-sponsored companies whose rules shape most conventional mortgages.
FCRA: Fair Credit Reporting Act — governs tenant-screening reports and requires an adverse-action notice if you deny based on one.
Federal Pacific panels: An old electrical panel brand known for fire-safety problems.
federal short-term rate: An interest rate the IRS sets, used to calculate penalties and interest.
FEMA: Federal Emergency Management Agency — publishes the flood maps that determine whether you need flood insurance.
FEMA flood map: A government map showing a property's flood risk, which you should check before buying.
FHA: Federal Housing Administration loans — owner-occupied, as little as 3.5% down (great for house hacking).
FHA loan: A government-backed mortgage that allows a very low down payment for a home you live in.
financed properties: The number of properties you have active mortgages on, which lenders cap (often at 10) for conventional loans.
financed-property count: The number of properties you have loans on, which can limit further conventional borrowing.
FinCEN: Financial Crimes Enforcement Network — the agency behind beneficial-ownership (BOI) reporting.
FINRA: Financial Industry Regulatory Authority — regulates brokers; a source on margin and SBLOC risk.
first lien: The primary loan against a property, which has first claim to be repaid if the property is sold or foreclosed.
fixed rate: An interest rate that stays the same for the life of the loan, so your payment never changes.
flood zone: A FEMA-designated area showing flood risk, where a high-risk zone can require mandatory flood insurance on a federally backed loan.
force appreciation: To raise a property's value on purpose through renovations rather than waiting for the market to lift it.
forced liquidation: When a broker sells your securities without your consent to cover a loan, often locking in losses and triggering taxes.
forced sale: Being compelled to sell an asset quickly, usually at a bad price, because you ran out of cash.
forced seller: Someone who must sell at a bad time, which can blow up a tax-deferral plan.
foreclosure: The legal process where a lender takes and sells your property because you failed to keep up the loan payments.
foreclosures: Properties being taken by a lender because the owner stopped paying the mortgage.
Form 1040-ES: The IRS form and vouchers used to pay estimated quarterly taxes.
Form 1099-NEC: An IRS form you send to report payments to non-employee service providers.
Form 3115: The IRS form used to fix a past accounting method error, such as missed depreciation, in the current year.
Form 8824: The IRS form you file to report a 1031 like-kind exchange.
Form FTB 3840: The California form for tracking a deferred gain from a 1031 exchange out of the state.
foundation: The structural base a building sits on; problems here are expensive to fix.
fractional interest: Owning a small share of a larger property along with other investors.
franchise tax: An annual fee some states charge a business just to exist there, such as California's 800-dollar minimum on LLCs.
Freddie Mac: A government-sponsored company, like Fannie Mae, that buys mortgages and helps set conventional loan standards.
free-and-clear: Owning a property outright with no mortgage or loan against it.
freeze the line: When a lender stops you from borrowing more on a HELOC, often because property values dropped.
front-load withholding: Pulling extra tax from your paycheck late in the year, which the IRS treats as paid evenly all year.
frozen credit market: A period when lenders largely stop making loans, so refinancing becomes impossible regardless of rate.
FTB: California Franchise Tax Board — issues Form 3840 for the state's 1031 'clawback.'
fully taxable disposition: Selling a property in a normal taxable sale, which frees up suspended losses.
galvanized supply lines: Old metal water pipes that corrode and clog over time.
Garn-St. Germain: The 1982 act that shields certain transfers (like into a living trust) from due-on-sale enforcement — generally not LLC transfers.
Garn-St. Germain Act: A federal statute listing transfers that cannot trigger a lender's due-on-sale clause, such as moving a home into a living trust.
GC: General contractor — runs your rehab; pay on a draw schedule and collect lien waivers.
general contractor: The lead person who manages a renovation and the workers on it.
gift tax: A federal tax on large transfers of money or property you make during life beyond the annual exclusion.
grantor: The person who creates a trust and places assets into it.
GRM: Gross rent multiplier = price ÷ annual rent. Lower means cheaper relative to the rent it produces.
gross income: All the rent and other income a property brings in before any expenses are subtracted.
gross income ~3x rent: A common requirement that an applicant earn at least three times the monthly rent.
gross rent: Total potential rent before vacancy and expenses are subtracted.
gross rent multiplier: Price ÷ annual rent — a fast comparative valuation tool that ignores expenses.
GST: Generation-skipping transfer tax, a tax on assets passed to grandchildren or later generations that skip a generation.
guardrails: Limits you set in advance to keep risky behavior from getting out of control.
hands-off portfolio: A set of investments that runs itself with almost no effort from you.
handymen: Skilled workers who handle smaller repair and maintenance jobs.
hard market: A period when insurance is expensive and hard to get, with rising premiums and carriers pulling out of risky areas.
hard money: Short-term, high-rate, asset-based loans used for flips and the buy/rehab stage of BRRRR.
headline number: A single eye-catching figure, like a high cap rate, that can hide real risks.
held for investment: Property you own to earn money or grow in value, not to live in personally.
HELOC: Home equity line of credit — a revolving second loan against your home equity, usually at a variable rate.
high-interest debt: Debt that charges a steep interest rate, like credit cards, that should be paid off first.
high-W-2 investor: An investor with a large salaried job income, who benefits especially from strategies that shelter that income.
HO-3: The standard homeowner policy for a home you live in — not valid on a rental (you need a landlord DP-3).
HOA: Homeowners association — dues and rules that affect a property's cost and use.
hold-and-1031: A plan to keep a property and use exchanges to defer tax rather than sell and pay it.
holding company: A parent LLC that owns your property LLCs but holds no real estate and runs no operations itself.
holding power: The ability to wait out a bad market instead of being forced to sell an illiquid asset — it comes from reserves and cash flow.
home equity: The share of your home you own outright, equal to its market value minus the mortgage balance.
home equity line of credit: A revolving second-lien credit line against your home equity; you pay interest only on what you draw.
house hacking: Living in one unit of a small multi (or renting rooms) to buy with low-down owner-occupied financing.
HSA: Health savings account — a triple-tax-advantaged account worth funding before stretching into more real estate.
HUD: US Department of Housing and Urban Development — enforces the Fair Housing Act.
HVAC: Heating, ventilation, and air conditioning — a major CapEx item; check its age before buying.
illiquid: Hard to turn into cash quickly without taking a price hit.
illiquid asset: Something you cannot sell quickly for cash without losing value, like a house.
improved land: Land that has been given basics like roads and utilities, making it costlier but easier to finance and resell.
improvement exchange: A 1031 variation where exchange funds pay to renovate or build on the new property.
income redundancy: Having more than one source of income so losing one does not wipe you out.
independent broker: An insurance agent who shops multiple carriers on your behalf rather than representing a single company.
index fund: A fund that automatically holds a broad basket of investments to mirror a market, at low cost.
index investing: Buying low-cost funds that track a whole market rather than picking individual stocks.
inflation-indexed: Adjusted each year to keep up with rising prices; some tax thresholds are not, so they catch more people over time.
insolvency: Owing more than you own, a condition that can let you exclude cancelled-debt income from taxes.
installment sale: Seller-financing that spreads your taxable gain across years to stay in lower brackets.
insurance broker: An independent agent who shops insurers to find the right coverage for you.
insurance premiums: The amount you pay for an insurance policy, usually yearly.
interest: The cost of borrowing money, charged by a lender as a percentage of the loan balance.
interest-only: A payment arrangement where you pay only the interest for a period and none of the loan balance, keeping payments low temporarily.
invested capital: The actual cash you put into a deal out of your own pocket.
investment-property loan: A mortgage for a property you will rent out, which costs more than a loan for a home you live in.
investor-friendly agent: A real estate agent who understands rental numbers and helps investors find profitable deals.
IRA: Individual retirement account — tax-advantaged; can hold real estate, with strict rules and UBIT/UDFI on leverage.
IRC: Internal Revenue Code — US federal tax law, cited as sections (e.g., §1031).
IRC section 121: The tax code section allowing tax-free gain on the sale of your main home up to set limits.
IRC section 453: The tax code section allowing installment sales to spread gain over the years payments are received.
irrevocable: Permanent and unable to be changed or undone once set up.
irrevocable trust: A trust you cannot change after creating it, which removes assets from your taxable estate but forfeits control.
IRS: Internal Revenue Service — the US federal tax authority.
IRS guidance: Official instructions the IRS issues explaining how to follow a tax law.
ISO: Incentive stock option — equity comp that can trigger AMT in a big exercise year.
ISO exercise: Using incentive stock options to buy company shares, which can trigger the alternative minimum tax.
itemized: Listing out individual deductions on your tax return instead of taking the standard flat amount.
itemized statement: A detailed written list explaining any deductions taken from a tenant's deposit.
K-1: The tax form reporting your share of income from a partnership or multi-member LLC.
key-person coverage: Life insurance tied to a crucial individual, used here so heirs can pay off loans if that person dies.
knob-and-tube wiring: An outdated, risky type of electrical wiring found in old homes.
land is never depreciable: The rule that you cannot take depreciation deductions on land itself, only on the building.
land trust: A revocable trust that holds title for privacy and to soften due-on-sale risk.
land vs building allocation: Splitting the purchase price between the non-depreciable land and the depreciable building.
landlord: The owner of a property who rents it out to tenants.
landlord coverage: Insurance designed for a property you rent out rather than live in.
landlord policy: Insurance designed for a rental property, also called a dwelling policy, which a regular homeowner's policy cannot replace.
landlord-friendly states: States where laws make it relatively quick and easy to evict a non-paying tenant.
lateral: The underground pipe connecting a property's plumbing to the main sewer line.
lead channels: The different sources you use to find potential property deals.
lead-based-paint disclosure: A required notice to tenants about possible lead paint in homes built before 1978.
lead-paint: Toxic old paint, banned in 1978, that requires disclosure and careful handling.
lease: A binding contract setting the terms under which a tenant rents a property from a landlord.
leases: The contracts that set the terms tenants agree to, including rent and length of stay.
leverage: Using borrowed money to control a larger asset. It amplifies returns and losses symmetrically.
leveraged property: Property bought partly with borrowed money, which can trigger special taxes inside an IRA.
levered: Measured after accounting for the loan used to buy the asset.
liability: A debt or financial obligation you owe to someone else.
liability silo: Isolating each property in its own entity so a lawsuit over one cannot reach the others.
liability veil: The legal separation that keeps an LLC owner personal assets safe from business lawsuits.
licensed, bonded, and insured: A contractor who is legally permitted, has a surety bond backing their work, and carries liability insurance.
lien: A legal claim against a property that must be paid off before the owner can sell with clear title.
lien waiver: A signed release from a contractor or sub confirming payment, protecting you from later liens.
lien waivers: Signed documents from contractors and suppliers confirming they have been paid and give up the right to lien your property.
liens: Legal claims against a property for unpaid debts that must be cleared before a clean sale.
lifetime exemption: The total amount you can pass to heirs over your life and at death free of federal estate and gift tax.
like-kind: For real estate, almost any US investment property qualifies as like-kind to any other.
limited liability company: A business structure that separates your personal assets from the business's debts and lawsuits while passing income through to your taxes.
liquidity: How easily and quickly you can turn something into spendable cash.
liquidity ladder: A ranked order of cash sources to draw on in a crisis, from immediately available cash down to less reliable credit lines.
live-in flip: Living in a home while you renovate it, then selling it for a tax-favored profit.
living trust: A revocable trust set up during your lifetime to hold assets, which can pass them on without probate.
LLC: Limited liability company — a pass-through entity that can shield your personal assets from a property lawsuit (if run correctly).
loan officer: A bank employee who handles your loan application.
loan-to-value: Loan ÷ property value — a key risk ratio that sets down payment and pricing.
long-term rent comps: Comparable rents for standard year-long leases in the area.
loss-of-rent: Coverage that pays your rental income while a unit is uninhabitable after a covered loss.
low-down-payment: Bought with only a small upfront cash amount.
LTV: Loan-to-value = loan ÷ property value. Drives your down payment, pricing, and whether you owe PMI.
MAGI: Modified adjusted gross income — AGI with some items added back; sets NIIT and passive-loss phase-outs.
maintenance requirement: The minimum collateral value you must keep in a margin or securities-backed account, below which the lender demands more.
maintenance reserve: Money set aside for routine, smaller repairs.
management LLC: A separate operating entity that runs the properties day to day for a fee but owns no real estate, absorbing operational lawsuits.
mansion tax: An extra tax some cities charge on the sale of higher-priced homes.
margin call: A demand for more collateral when your portfolio falls; if unmet, the broker can sell your securities without notice.
margin loan: Borrowing against your brokerage holdings; unlike an SBLOC, it can be used to buy more securities.
margin of safety: A built-in buffer in your numbers, such as keeping loan and coverage ratios conservative, to absorb bad surprises.
margin-call: A demand from a lender for more cash or collateral when the value backing a loan drops.
market rent: The going rent a unit could realistically command in its area.
material participation: Being involved enough (e.g., 100+ hrs and more than anyone else, or 500 hrs) to treat an activity as non-passive.
materially participate: To be involved in a business enough, by hours or tests, that its losses count against your other income.
materialman's lien: A lien filed by an unpaid materials supplier — like a mechanic's lien, it can attach to your title.
maturity: The date a loan must be fully paid off or refinanced.
maximally-levered: Carrying as much debt as possible, which makes a portfolio fragile.
mechanic's lien: A claim an unpaid contractor or sub can place on your property — even if you already paid the general contractor.
mechanics lien: A claim an unpaid contractor or supplier can place on your property even if you already paid the general contractor.
membership interest: An owner's stake in an LLC, the equivalent of shares in a corporation.
membership interests: Ownership shares in an LLC, which a holding company can own to control its child LLCs.
MFJ: Married filing jointly — the tax status with the higher income thresholds (e.g., $250k NIIT).
MLS: Multiple listing service — the on-market property database; at today's prices these rarely cash-flow without work.
mortgage: A loan used to buy real estate, with the property itself serving as collateral.
mortgage broker: A professional who shops multiple lenders to find you a mortgage.
mortgage interest: The interest you pay on a property loan, which is often tax deductible.
motivated seller: An owner eager to sell quickly, often willing to accept a lower price.
multi-member LLC: An LLC with more than one owner, which generally provides stronger asset protection than a single-member one.
multi-state filings: Filing tax returns in more than one state because you own property across states.
multifamily: A residential property with more than one rentable unit, like a duplex or apartment building.
mutual fund: A pooled investment that buys many stocks or bonds on behalf of its investors.
named peril: Insurance that covers only the specific causes of loss listed in the policy, with everything else excluded.
national origin: A protected class based on the country a person or their ancestors came from.
negative cash flow: When a propertys expenses and loan payments exceed its rental income, draining money each month.
negative-cash-flow reserve: Money set aside to cover months when a property loses money.
net investment income: Income from investments such as interest, dividends, capital gains, and passive rentals.
net investment income tax: A 3.8% surtax on passive rental income and non-1031 gains above $200k/$250k MAGI.
net operating income: Gross rent minus vacancy and operating expenses, before debt service. The basis for cap rate and DSCR.
net rental cash flow: The profit from your rentals after every expense and the mortgage are paid.
net worth: Everything you own minus everything you owe; your total financial value.
NFIP: National Flood Insurance Program — the main source of flood coverage (excluded from standard policies).
NIIT: Net investment income tax — a 3.8% surtax on investment income once MAGI tops $200k single / $250k married.
NIIT-exempt: Not subject to the 3.8 percent investment income tax.
NOI: Net operating income — gross rent minus vacancy and operating expenses, before the mortgage payment.
non-cash deduction: A tax write-off that lowers your taxable income without you actually spending money that year.
non-passive: Income or loss from an activity you actively run, which can freely offset wages and other income.
non-purpose loan: A loan against your investments that can be used for almost anything except buying more securities.
non-recourse: A loan limited to the collateral — the lender cannot pursue your other assets (absent bad-boy carve-outs).
nonresident return: A state tax return you file for income earned in a state where you do not live.
OBBBA: The One Big Beautiful Bill Act (2025) — made bonus depreciation, the QBI deduction, and the ~$15M estate exemption permanent.
occupancy requirement: A loan rule that you must actually live in the property for a set period, often about a year.
off-market: Properties for sale that are not listed publicly on the MLS, where competition is thinner.
off-market deal flow: A steady supply of properties for sale that are not publicly listed, where competition is thinner.
offering memo: The marketing document a seller provides describing a property and its claimed numbers.
offset: To use a loss or deduction to cancel out income so you pay less tax.
on-market inventory: Properties publicly listed for sale, where competition is highest.
One Big Beautiful Bill Act: A federal tax law signed July 4 2025 that updated depreciation, deductions, and other real estate tax rules.
OP units: Operating-partnership units — received in a 721 exchange/UPREIT; convertible to REIT shares but taxable when sold.
open peril: Insurance that covers all causes of loss except those specifically excluded, broader than named-peril coverage.
operating agreement: The internal contract that spells out how an LLC is owned and run, important for keeping its liability protection valid.
operating expenses: Taxes, insurance, management, maintenance, utilities, HOA — owed whether occupied or not (the mortgage is separate).
operating LLC: An entity that handles leasing, rent, maintenance, and vendors but holds no appreciating property of its own.
operating partnership: The partnership inside a REIT that holds properties and issues OP units to contributors.
operating reserves: Cash kept on hand to run a property and cover normal ups and downs.
opportunity zone: A program that defers capital gains reinvested into a Qualified Opportunity Fund; a 10-year hold can make new appreciation tax-free.
ordinary income: Regular income like wages and salary, taxed at standard rates.
out of pocket: The cash you actually spend yourself on a deal, separate from borrowed money.
over-leverage: Carrying too much debt relative to your assets and cash, leaving no cushion for a downturn.
owner-occupant: A buyer who will live in the property, eligible for better financing terms than an investor.
owner-occupied: A property the buyer lives in, which qualifies for cheaper loans than a pure rental.
owner-occupied financing: A mortgage with better terms because the borrower will live in the property.
owner-paid utilities: Utility bills the landlord covers rather than the tenant.
P&I: Principal and interest — the core mortgage payment (excludes taxes and insurance).
PAL: Pledged Asset Line — Schwab's name for a securities-backed line of credit (SBLOC).
paper loss: A loss that appears on your tax return from deductions like depreciation, even while you have real positive cash flow.
parent LLC: The top entity in a multi-LLC structure that owns the ownership stakes in the property-holding child LLCs.
park title: To temporarily hold legal ownership of a property through a third party during a reverse exchange.
partial-release clause: A loan provision that lets you sell or free one property from a blanket loan without paying off the whole loan.
pass-through taxation: A tax setup where business income flows directly to the owner's personal tax return, avoiding a separate corporate tax.
passive: Income or activity where you are mostly a hands-off investor rather than an active worker.
passive activity loss: Rental losses that normally only offset passive income unless you actively/materially participate.
passive activity losses: Losses from investments you do not actively run, which can usually only offset other passive income.
passive income: Earnings from investments you do not actively manage day to day, like most rentals.
passive investing: A hands-off approach, like buying index funds, that needs little ongoing work.
passive vs active: The tax distinction between income you earn without ongoing work and income from a business you run hands-on.
passive-loss release: When trapped passive losses are finally freed up to offset income, usually upon a taxable sale.
payment shock: A sudden jump in your required payment, such as when a HELOC switches from interest-only to full repayment.
payroll tax: The 15.3 percent tax on wages funding Social Security and Medicare.
per-door: Measured per rental unit; one door equals one unit.
per-property liability coverage: Insurance on each rental that pays if someone is injured or sues over something that happens at that property.
permissible purpose: A legally valid reason required before you may pull someone's credit report.
permits: Official government approvals required before doing certain construction, the absence of which can cause problems at sale, refinance, or insurance claim.
personal guarantee: A promise you sign personally to repay a loan, which means you are on the hook even if the loan is in your LLC's name.
personal residence: The home you actually live in, as opposed to an investment property.
pet rent: An extra monthly charge for a tenant who keeps a pet.
phase-down: A gradual reduction of a tax benefit over time.
phaseout: The income or spending level at which a tax benefit gradually shrinks to zero.
pierce the veil: A court action that lets creditors reach an owner's personal assets when the LLC was operated improperly.
piercing the veil: A court setting aside LLC protection to hold you personally liable, often due to commingled funds.
placed in service: The date a property is ready and available for use, which starts its depreciation clock.
pledged assets: Investments you put up as collateral to secure a loan, which the lender can seize if you fail to repay.
PM: Property manager / property management — runs units day-to-day (typically 8–10% of rent).
PMI: Private mortgage insurance — an added cost when your loan-to-value is high (a low down payment).
POA: Power of attorney — lets a trusted person sign for your LLCs and access accounts if you are incapacitated.
pocket listings: Properties an agent quietly markets without putting them on the public MLS.
points: Upfront fees on a loan, each point equal to one percent of the loan amount.
polybutylene: An old plumbing pipe material prone to failure and leaks.
portability: A rule letting a surviving spouse inherit and use their late spouses unused estate-tax exemption.
portfolio loan: A loan the lender keeps on its own books, allowing flexible underwriting past conventional limits.
portfolio loans: Loans a lender keeps on its own books, with flexible rules, useful for investors with many properties.
postnup: A postnuptial agreement signed during marriage that, like a prenup, can shield specified assets in a divorce.
pre-1978: Built before 1978, when lead paint was banned, triggering special disclosure rules.
pre-listings: Properties shared with select buyers before they officially hit the market.
pre-tax cash flow: The cash profit a property produces before income taxes are applied.
premium: The amount you pay an insurer for coverage, usually annually.
prenup: A prenuptial agreement signed before marriage that can protect separately owned investment assets from a future divorce split.
price correction: A meaningful drop in market prices after a period of rising values.
primary residence: The home you live in most of the time.
primary residence exclusion: A rule letting you exclude a large amount of gain from tax when you sell the home you live in.
prime: Short for the prime rate, the benchmark banks use to set rates on loans like a HELOC.
prime rate: A benchmark interest rate banks use as a starting point for many consumer loans, which moves up and down with the broader market.
principal: The original amount of money borrowed on a loan, separate from the interest charged on it.
prior-year AGI: Your adjusted gross income from last year, used to set safe-harbor payment rules.
private lender: An individual or non-bank source who lends you money, often quickly and on flexible terms.
pro forma: A seller projection of income and expenses — routinely optimistic, so underwrite your own conservative numbers.
probate: The court process of validating a will and distributing a deceased persons assets, which trusts can help avoid.
proceeds: The money you receive from selling a property.
professional inspection: A paid expert examination of a property's condition before you buy.
prohibited transaction: A banned dealing in a retirement account, like using the property yourself, that can disqualify the whole account.
property class: A grading of a neighborhood and property quality from A (best) to D (roughest).
property manager: A person or company you hire to run rentals day-to-day for a fee.
property taxes: Annual taxes a local government charges based on a property's value.
property value: The estimated market worth of a property.
PropStream: A data tool investors use to find property owner information and leads.
protected classes: Groups the law shields from housing discrimination, like race, religion, sex, and disability.
QBI: Qualified business income — up to a 20% deduction (§199A) for a rental run as a trade or business.
QI: Short for Qualified Intermediary, the company that holds your funds during a 1031 exchange.
QOF: Qualified Opportunity Fund — the vehicle you invest a capital gain into for Opportunity Zone tax benefits.
QOZ: Qualified Opportunity Zone — a designated area where reinvested gains get deferral and potential tax-free growth.
QROF: Qualified Rural Opportunity Fund — an Opportunity Zone fund for rural areas, with a larger basis step-up.
qualified business income: The eligible profit from a business that can get the 20 percent pass-through deduction.
qualified intermediary: A required middleman who holds 1031 sale proceeds so you never take constructive receipt of the cash.
Qualified Opportunity Fund: An investment fund that puts money into opportunity zones to unlock the tax breaks.
Qualified Opportunity Zone: A designated area where reinvesting capital gains can defer and reduce future tax.
rate premium: The extra interest charged on a riskier loan compared with a standard one.
rate resets: Moments when an adjustable loan recalculates its interest rate, often raising your payment.
raw land: Undeveloped land with no roads, utilities, or buildings, which is cheap per acre but hard to finance.
real estate attorney: A lawyer specializing in property matters like entities, leases, and evictions.
real estate exposure: How much of your total wealth is tied to real estate, including the debt on it.
real estate professional status: A tax status (750+ hrs, majority of your work in real estate) that lets rental losses offset W-2 income.
real property: Land and anything permanently attached to it, like buildings; basically real estate.
realize capital gains: To trigger a taxable profit by actually selling an investment that has risen in value.
reasonable accommodations: Reasonable changes to rules or properties a landlord must consider for a tenant's disability.
reasonable salary: A fair market wage an S-corp owner must pay themselves before taking lower-taxed distributions.
reassessed: Re-valued by the tax authority, often to your purchase price, which can raise your property tax bill.
recapture: At sale, the IRS taxes back the depreciation you claimed (or should have) at up to 25%.
recognize gain: To report a profit on your tax return in a given year so it becomes taxable.
recordation tax: A tax charged for officially recording a property deed or sale.
recourse: A loan where the lender can pursue you personally for any shortfall after foreclosure.
recycled capital: Money you pull back out of one property (through refinancing or equity) to fund the next purchase.
redemption periods: A legal window after a foreclosure during which the former owner can reclaim the property.
refinance: Replacing an existing loan with a new one, often to pull out cash or get a better rate.
Reg-T: A Federal Reserve rule that sets how much you can initially borrow on margin against securities.
rehab overruns: Renovation costs that come in higher than budgeted.
REIA: Real estate investors association — local meetups for deal flow, contractors, lenders, and referrals.
REIT: Real estate investment trust — gives real-estate exposure with stock-like liquidity and no management.
REITs: Companies whose shares let you invest in real estate through a brokerage account.
remaining life: How many years a major system, like a roof or HVAC, has left before replacement.
rent comps: Recent rents for similar nearby units, used to estimate what a property can charge.
rental activity: A category under tax rules that is normally passive, unless short stays make it a trade or business.
rental income haircut: The lender practice of counting only part (about 75 percent) of your rent as qualifying income.
rental services: Hours of work like maintenance, management, and leasing that count toward rental safe harbors.
renters insurance: A tenant's own policy covering their belongings and their liability, which you can require as a lease condition.
Rentometer: A tool that estimates fair market rent for a property.
REO: Real estate owned — bank-owned property after foreclosure; can be discounted but higher-risk.
repair vs improvement: The distinction between a fix you deduct now and an upgrade you must depreciate over time.
repair-and-vacancy buffer: Cash set aside per property to cover repairs and stretches when it sits empty.
repairs: Fixing things that break or wear out in a property, an ongoing cost of ownership.
repayment period: The later phase of a HELOC when you can no longer borrow and must pay back both principal and interest.
replacement cost: Insurance that pays what it costs to rebuild or replace property today, without deducting for age or wear.
replacement property: The new property you buy in a 1031 exchange to replace the one you sold.
reporting agency: The company that supplied the credit or background report.
REPS: Real estate professional status — 750+ hrs and over half your work in real estate; makes rental losses non-passive.
reserves: Cash set aside for vacancies, repairs, and shortfalls so you are never forced to sell at a bad time.
resets your whole mortgage: A refinance that replaces your entire existing loan, so you lose your old rate and start over at today's rate.
retail buyers: Ordinary buyers purchasing a home to live in, not investors hunting for deals.
return metrics: The calculations used to measure how profitable an investment is.
return on equity: The profit you earn measured against the actual cash you put in.
Revenue Procedure 2000-37: The IRS guidance that established the rules for reverse 1031 exchanges.
reverse exchange: A 1031 variation where you buy the new property before selling the old one.
revocable living trust: A trust you control and can change during life that avoids probate and keeps the step-up but offers no asset protection.
revocable trust: A trust you can change or cancel while alive, often used to hold property for privacy and easier transfer.
revolving: A type of credit you can borrow, repay, and re-borrow repeatedly up to a set limit, like a credit card.
risk budget: A decided-in-advance limit on how much risk you are willing to take before you act.
risk-adjusted return: How good a return is once you account for how much risk was taken to get it.
ROI: Return on investment — profit relative to what you put in.
Roth: A type of retirement account where you pay tax now so future growth and withdrawals are tax-free.
routine-maintenance safe harbor: A rule letting you deduct upkeep you expect to do more than once over a building life.
run comps: To look up recent sales or rents of similar nearby properties to estimate value.
runway: The amount of time you have to reach a goal before money or options run out.
S-corp: An S corporation tax election — useful on a management LLC to cut self-employment tax, but never for holding appreciating real estate.
S-corp election: A tax choice that lets a business be taxed as an S corporation, which can reduce certain self-employment taxes.
safe harbor: A clear IRS rule that, if you follow it, protects you from penalties or challenges.
SBLOC: Securities-backed line of credit — borrow against your brokerage portfolio without selling it (and realizing gains).
Schedule C: The tax schedule for an active business; substantial hotel-like STR services can push you here, adding SE tax.
Schedule E: The tax schedule where rental income and expenses (including full mortgage interest) are reported.
scope of work: A written, detailed list of every repair and improvement to be done, used to get comparable bids from contractors.
screening filters: Quick tests to rule out bad deals fast, not a reason on their own to buy.
screening standard: A consistent written set of criteria applied to every rental applicant.
SE tax: Self-employment tax (15.3%) on active business income; an S-corp election on a management LLC can reduce it.
seasoning: The time a lender makes you own a property before refinancing at its new appraised value (often 6–12 months).
second lien: A loan secured by a property that sits behind the main mortgage, so it gets paid only after the first loan in a foreclosure.
section 1014: The tax code section that gives heirs a fresh, higher basis equal to the value at the owner death.
Section 121: The tax exclusion letting you avoid tax on up to 250,000 or 500,000 of gain on a home you lived in.
Section 121 capital-gains exclusion: A tax break that lets you avoid tax on much of the gain from selling a home you lived in.
section 179 expensing: A rule letting businesses deduct the full cost of certain equipment in the year of purchase, up to a limit.
section 199A: The tax code section giving a deduction of up to 20 percent of qualified business income.
section 280A(g): The tax code provision behind the Augusta Rule allowing 14 days of tax-free home rental income.
section 453A interest charge: An extra interest charge owed on very large installment sale balances.
section 469: The tax code section governing passive activity rules, including what counts as a rental.
section 481(a): A catch-up adjustment that corrects prior accounting errors in the current tax year.
section 514(c)(9): A tax code provision that exempts a Solo 401(k) from the debt-financed income tax.
Section 8 vouchers: Government rent-assistance payments that help low-income tenants afford housing.
securities-backed line of credit: A loan against your stocks/funds; proceeds cannot buy securities and retirement accounts cannot be pledged.
security deposits: Money collected from a tenant upfront to cover potential damage or unpaid rent.
self-directed IRA: A retirement account that lets you hold alternative assets like rental property.
self-employment tax: The 15.3 percent tax that self-employed people pay to cover Social Security and Medicare.
seller financing: An arrangement where the property seller acts as the lender and you make payments to them instead of a bank.
seller-finance: When the seller acts as the lender and the buyer pays them over time instead of getting a bank loan.
series LLC: One LLC with internal cells that wall off assets from each other; cheaper, but largely untested in court.
service the debt: To make the loan payments on time out of the income a property produces.
services customary to occupancy: Basic guest services like cleaning between stays and Wi-Fi that keep a rental out of self-employment tax.
seven sins rules: Restrictions on a Delaware Statutory Trust that bar it from refinancing or improving its property.
sewer scope: Sending a camera down the sewer line to check for hidden, costly damage.
short sale: Selling a property for less than the loan balance with the lender's approval, often instead of foreclosure.
short-term rental: A property rented out for short stays, like a vacation rental, often with special tax treatment.
side agreements: Extra arrangements between landlord and tenant outside the written lease.
signing in the entity's name and capacit: Signing contracts as a manager of the LLC rather than personally, to keep the liability shield intact.
single-member LLC: An LLC owned by just one person, which in many states offers weaker legal protection than one with multiple owners.
sleeve: A defined slice of your overall portfolio set aside for one purpose or asset type.
small multifamily: A residential building with roughly two to four rental units.
small-taxpayer safe harbor: A rule letting owners of lower-value buildings deduct a limited amount of repairs each year.
SOFR: Secured Overnight Financing Rate — the benchmark many SBLOC and variable rates are priced over.
Solo 401(k): A one-participant 401(k) for the self-employed; unlike an IRA it is exempt from UDFI on leveraged real estate.
source of income: Where a tenant's money comes from, like a housing voucher, which some places protect from discrimination.
Special Flood Hazard Area: A high-risk flood zone on FEMA maps where flood insurance is mandatory if you have a federally backed mortgage.
special-form: An insurance term for broad open-peril coverage that protects against all risks except those specifically listed as excluded.
speculative: An investment made mainly betting on price appreciation rather than steady income, carrying higher risk.
sponsor fees: Charges paid to the company that organizes and manages an investment like a DST.
stabilized: A property that is fully renovated, rented, and operating normally, making it eligible for standard financing.
stabilized asset: A property that is fully rented and running smoothly with predictable income.
state 1031 nonconformity: When a state does not follow federal 1031 rules, so you may still owe state tax.
state-specific lease: A rental contract written to follow the laws of the property's particular state.
statutory damages: Penalties set by law that you owe automatically for breaking a rule, regardless of actual harm.
steering: Illegally guiding applicants toward or away from certain units or areas based on a protected trait.
step-up: The reset of cost basis to market value at death that wipes out a lifetime of deferred gain.
step-up in basis: At death, heirs reset the cost basis to market value — permanently erasing the deferred gain and depreciation recapture.
step-up in basis at death: When you die, your property value resets to its current market value for your heirs, wiping out the built-up taxable gain.
stop-scaling trigger: A condition you set in advance that tells you to stop buying and start reducing risk.
STR: Short-term rental (e.g., Airbnb). With an average stay of 7 days or less plus material participation, its losses can offset W-2 income.
STR strategy: A short-term-rental tax approach that can unlock special deductions.
straight-line depreciation: Spreading a building deduction evenly in equal amounts over a set number of years.
stress test: Modeling how your portfolio would survive a severe combined downturn to check whether you are over-leveraged.
subcontractor: A specialized worker hired by the general contractor to handle one part of a job, like framing or plumbing.
subsidies: Government help that lowers your health-insurance cost, which shrinks as your income rises.
substantial services: Hotel-like extras such as daily cleaning or meals that can turn a rental into a self-employment business.
successor manager: The person named in advance to take over running an LLC if the current manager dies or becomes unable to serve.
surplus lines: Specialty insurance from non-standard carriers used to cover risks that ordinary insurers will not write.
surtax: An additional tax charged on top of the regular tax.
suspended losses: Losses you could not use this year that carry forward to offset income in future years.
swap till you drop: A strategy of doing 1031 exchanges your whole life so the tax is never paid, then erased at death.
sweat equity: Value you add by doing work yourself, which is not allowed inside a self-directed retirement account.
tactic: A specific move or technique used to pursue your investing goals.
tax avoidance: Legally arranging your affairs to minimize tax, as opposed to illegal tax evasion.
tax shelter: A legal way to reduce or delay the taxes owed on income.
tax strategy: The legal planning of your finances to pay as little tax as the law allows.
tax treatment: How the tax rules apply to an investment, which can help or hurt your net return.
tax-advantaged: Accounts or investments that get special tax breaks, like a 401(k) or IRA.
tax-deferred: Describing income or growth where you put off paying the tax until later.
tax-free liquidity: Getting usable cash, usually by borrowing, without triggering a taxable sale.
taxable brokerage: A regular investment account, not a retirement account, where gains and income are taxed in the year earned.
taxable-bond interest: Interest income from bonds that is subject to income tax.
TCJA: Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (2017) — set the $750k mortgage-interest cap and limited 1031 to real property.
tenant: A person who rents and occupies a property owned by someone else.
tenant screening: Checking applicants' income, credit, and history before renting to them.
tenant-friendly jurisdictions: Places where laws favor tenants and evictions can take many months.
tenant-occupied building: A property that already has renters living in it when you buy.
testers: People who pose as applicants to check whether a landlord discriminates.
the spread: The gap in return between two deals, which often reflects extra risk rather than free profit.
the turn: The work and cost of getting a unit ready for the next tenant after one leaves.
time horizon: The length of time you plan to invest before you need to reach your goal.
timing benefit: A tax break that moves deductions earlier rather than eliminating the tax entirely.
tired landlords: Landlords worn out by managing properties who may be ready to sell.
title: The legal ownership of a property and the document or record proving who owns it.
title issues: Legal problems with a property's ownership record, like unpaid liens, that can block a clean sale.
title search: A check of public records to confirm clear ownership and find any liens or claims.
total cash invested: All the money you personally put into a deal, including down payment and costs.
total income: All the money a property brings in, from rent plus any extra sources.
total return: An investment's full gain including both price growth and income like rent or dividends.
trade or business: An activity run regularly to make a profit, which unlocks certain tax benefits.
transaction costs: The fees and expenses you pay to buy or sell an asset.
transfer tax: A tax charged when property changes ownership, usually a percentage of the price.
Treasury guidance: Official rules from the US Treasury explaining how to apply a tax law.
trustee: The person or entity that legally holds and manages property in a trust on behalf of the beneficiary.
turnover: How often tenants leave and must be replaced, which costs time and money each time.
UBIT: Unrelated business income tax — tax a retirement account owes on debt-financed (UDFI) or active-business income.
UDFI: Unrelated debt-financed income — the leveraged share of IRA real-estate income that gets taxed. Solo 401(k)s are exempt.
umbrella coverage: Extra liability insurance that sits on top of your other policies for big claims.
umbrella policy: Extra liability coverage ($1–5M) stacked on your auto and landlord policies — cheap and high-leverage protection.
under contract: Having a signed agreement to buy a property, before the sale is finalized.
underpayment penalty: A charge the IRS adds when you did not pay enough tax during the year.
underwater: Owing more on a property than it is currently worth.
underwrite: To carefully analyze a deal's numbers to judge whether it is sound and worth buying.
underwriter: The person or system that reviews a loan application and decides whether to approve it.
underwriting: The process a lender uses to review and decide whether to approve a loan and on what terms.
unincorporated service provider: A vendor who is not a corporation, such as a sole proprietor you must issue a 1099 to.
unleveraged: Owned without any borrowed money against it.
unlevered: Measured without using any borrowed money.
unlevered cap rate: A return measure that assumes you bought the property with cash and no loan.
unrecaptured section 1250 gain: The portion of your sale profit tied to past depreciation, taxed at up to 25 percent.
UPREIT: Umbrella partnership REIT — the structure behind a 721 exchange into operating-partnership units.
vacancy: The share of potential rent lost to empty units; underwrite 5–10% (more in soft markets).
vacancy clause: A policy provision that voids or limits coverage once a property sits empty for a period, common during BRRRR rehabs.
vacancy loss: The rent you lose while a unit sits empty between tenants.
vacant-property policy: Insurance for a property that is empty, since standard landlord coverage can lapse once a building is unoccupied.
value-adds: Properties you can improve to raise their value or rent.
variable rate: An interest rate that can change over time, usually tied to a benchmark like prime, so your payment can rise or fall.
veil piercing: When a court disregards your LLC and reaches you personally — usually from commingling or undercapitalization.
verified comps: Comparable property numbers you have independently confirmed rather than taken on faith.
volatility: How much an investment's value swings up and down over time.
W-2: The standard employee income that lenders trust; a W-2 is the tax form your employer issues.
W-2 cliff: The sudden loss of employee benefits and easy financing when you quit a job to invest full-time.
W-2 income: The salary or wages you earn as an employee, reported on a W-2 form.
W-2 withholding: Tax taken directly from your employee wages throughout the year.
W-9: A form you collect from a vendor with their tax ID so you can later issue them a 1099.
water heater: The appliance that heats a building's water, a costly item to replace.
waterfall: An ordered priority list that decides where your money goes first, second, and so on.
wholesaler: Someone who puts a property under contract and assigns it to an investor for a fee.
wholesalers: People who lock up a property under contract and then sell that contract to an investor for a fee.
wind/flood/wildfire markets: Areas prone to storms, flooding, or fires, where insurance costs more and can spike.
withholding: Tax automatically taken out of your paycheck and sent to the IRS for you.
yield: The income an investment pays out each year as a percentage of its price.
§1014: The tax-code section for the step-up in basis at death.
§1031: The like-kind exchange section that defers capital-gains tax on investment real estate.
§121: The primary-residence capital-gains exclusion ($250k single / $500k married).
§1250: The section governing depreciation recapture on real property (taxed up to 25%).
§179: First-year expensing of certain business property (up to $2.5M for 2025).
§199A: The 20% qualified-business-income (QBI) deduction, made permanent by OBBBA.
§280A: The section behind the Augusta rule (14-day tax-free home rental).
§453A: An interest charge on very large installment-sale deferrals (over $5M outstanding).
§469: The passive-activity-loss rules that the STR and REPS strategies work around.
§481(a): The catch-up adjustment (via Form 3115) that lets you claim depreciation you previously missed.
§514(c)(9): The provision that exempts Solo 401(k)s from UDFI tax on leveraged real estate.
